claims.claim: Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units carefully.
The government should limit rent increases within tenancies and add longer security of tenure.
The government should not impose hard caps on rent levels.
First-generation rent controls (hard caps on levels) cause consistent supply contraction.
Second-generation rent controls (caps on increases within tenancies) have small or null stock effects.
Hong Kong's 2021 ordinance is second-generation, explaining stock growth from 100,800 units in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025.
The stability of Hong Kong's rent control is not evidence that a binding cap is safe; it shows the existing instrument does not bind at the point of pain.
The think-tank argument that 'capacity exists for more control' misreads a non-binding instrument's stability as proof that a binding one would behave the same way.
The estimated elasticity of SDU-type supply to controlled rents is 0.31 to 0.48, meaning a 10 percent cap-induced reduction removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years.

A modelled 15 percent cut in initial rents would transfer about 900 dollars a month to incumbents while leaving 3,000 to 4,000 households per year unable to enter the segment, mostly new arrivals and newly formed households.

Berlin illustrates the mechanism: initial-offer rents fell, listing supply contracted within a year as owners withheld or rerouted flats, and when the law fell, suppressed increases released above the pre-cap trend line.
The tenants a cap protects are those already inside; the bill goes to those still outside.
Median rent growth was 3.1 percent in 2021 to 2023, slower than the earlier 6.8 percent, but still higher than general private rent growth of 1.7 percent.
Rent burden rose from 31 to 34 percent.
The 2021 ordinance was too weak, and a modest tightening of the increase limit is justified.
Mr Chan, asked what would help most, does not name rent; he names the waiting list, and says he would accept any rent to leave if the queue were three years instead of five and a half.
The NGO survey of 440 households found 61 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year tenure security and 74 percent for a faster public-housing offer.
The segment is tight because the queue is long; rent caps treat the price symptom of a quantity problem.
Enforcement effort spent on policing rents is not spent on inspecting fire and ventilation conditions, where harm is immediate.
Hong Kong should tighten rent control by lowering the allowed increases and extending tenure security.

[2] (typed) I guess I'm least sure that tightening rent control actually helps tenants rather than hurting them. I would need evidence, ideally data, plus a counter-view.
[4] (pick reason) D2 has actual rent data, D6 models whether rent control hurts supply, D11 gives the tenant side and an alternative to caps
[12] (typed) I read the data. Stock kept growing after the 2021 ordinance, so mild control did not make landlords leave. But rent burden still went up. Is that a problem for my argument?
[14] (typed) I think hard caps are risky but a small tightening of increase limits is fine, and the NGO says security of tenure matters more than caps.
[16] (typed) My claim: Hong Kong should tighten, but only second-generation controls (limits on increases within tenancies) plus longer tenure security, not hard caps. D6 says hard caps shrink stock but increase-limits have small or null effects, and D2 shows stock grew after 2021.
[18] (typed) A counter-view is that rent burden still worsened from 31 to 34 percent even under the ordinance, so maybe the ordinance was too weak.
[20] (typed) I agree hard caps could make owners leave, and D6 supports that for first-generation controls. That is why I only want limits on increases, which D6 says have small or null effects on stock.
[22] (typed) I will argue mainly for tenure security plus increase limits, since D11 says 61 percent would trade rent for three-year security.
